title: Git rebase
idea: `git rebase` replays your branch's commits on top of another branch, giving a straight history. The replayed commits are copies with new hashes.

analogy.text: You drafted chapters from a master copy. The master changes, so you retype your chapters onto the new version rather than attaching a note.
analogy.breaks: Colleagues holding your old chapters now hold copies that no longer match.

points: On a feature branch, `git rebase main` replays its commits on top of `main`.
Each replayed commit gets a new parent, so it gets a new hash.
A conflict pauses the replay: fix the file, `git add`, then `git rebase --continue`.
Rebase only commits you have not shared; teammates' copies of them would stop matching.

steps.caption: `about` branches from A and gets two commits, B and C.
Meanwhile `main` moves on to D. The two branches have diverged.
`git rebase main`, run on `about`, copies B and C on top of D. B′ and C′ are new commits; the originals fade.
`main` can now fast-forward to C′: a straight line, and no merge commit.

code.title: Rebase, then fast-forward
code.caption: Real Git output; hashes are fixed in this recording. Compare the two graphs: same pages, new hashes.

walk.text: Create `site` with one commit on `main`: the home page.
On a new branch `about`, commit two more pages.
Back on `main`, commit a different page. The branches diverge.
The graph forks: `about` has two commits, `main` has one.
Switch to `about` and rebase it onto `main`. Git replays both commits.
Same two pages, but new hashes, stacked on the contact page. One straight line.
On `main`, the merge is a fast-forward: no merge commit.

code.title: Abort a rebase
code.caption: Both branches change one line, so the rebase stops. Backing out is safe.

walk.text: Create `menu` with one commit, as on the merge page.
`main` changes the same line, so a conflict is certain.
The rebase stops while replaying that commit and prints `CONFLICT`, with hints.
`--abort` ends the rebase and restores the branch as it was.
The log shows the original commit again, with its original hash.

pitfalls: Do not rebase `main` or any branch teammates have pulled; their copies would diverge.
A rebased, already-pushed branch needs a force push; prefer `--force-with-lease`, on your own branch only.
Start from a clean `git status`; by default Git refuses to rebase with uncommitted changes.

quiz.q: What does the last command print? Options list the lines top to bottom.
quiz.code:
# main has one commit: base
git switch -c x
echo 1 > x.txt && git add x.txt && git commit -m X
git switch main
echo 2 > m.txt && git add m.txt && git commit -m M
git switch x
git rebase main
git log --format=%s
quiz.why: Rebase replays X on top of M, so X becomes the newest commit. `git log` lists newest first, and no merge commit exists.

takeaway: Rebase your own unpublished commits to tidy history; never rewrite shared ones.

starters: When should I choose rebase instead of merge?
How do I undo a rebase that already finished?
